p: Every Australian knows about the drop bear and pretty much every visitor hears about it within a day of landing. The story is that it's a bigger, meat-eating cousin of the koala that sits dead still in a gum tree over a bush track and then drops onto the head of whoever walks underneath.

The whole trick is the delivery. Locals tell it with a totally straight face, throw in little details that make it sound real (the leaves rustle first, they hunt in pairs, they only go after tourists) and then wait for the visitor to look up at the next tree. Hostels, tour guides, park rangers and a whole lot of people online keep the bit going and honestly I love that a whole country is in on it.

Nobody knows who made it up. The earliest printed mention anyone has found is in a 1967 Australian Army newspaper warning about "a dreaded Drop Bear", so it looks like they were already using it on new recruits. Through the 70s and 80s it spread around bush camps, backpacker hostels and newspaper humour columns.

Then the serious folks got involved. The Australian Museum has a deadpan entry for the drop bear with the scientific name Thylarctos plummetus. Australian Geographic ran it as an April Fool's story. And in 2012 a University of Tasmania surveyor named Volker Janssen published a tongue-in-cheek paper in the journal Australian Geographer about tracking drop bears with GPS, which found they prefer going after people with foreign accents. Peer reviewed, folks.

Koalas aren't dangerous the way the joke makes out. They only eat eucalyptus leaves and they sleep most of the day. They can scratch and bite pretty hard if you grab one or corner it, and every so often one falls out of a tree or climbs down when you don't expect it, which is probably part of why the joke works so well.

Here's the fun part though. Australia really did have a tree-climbing marsupial predator. Thylacoleo carnifex, the marsupial lion, was about the size of a leopard with a nasty bite and huge thumb claws, and it probably hunted from the trees. It died out tens of thousands of years ago so nobody was around to tell stories about it, but drop bear fans love bringing it up.

sections.h: How to protect yourself (according to Australians)
p: The advice depends on who's telling it. The usual tips are Vegemite or toothpaste behind your ears, forks stuck in your hair so the bear gets a mouthful of metal, walking with a friend who's shorter than you and talking in an Australian accent, since apparently drop bears leave locals alone.
If somebody gives you all of that advice at once and then can't keep a straight face, congrats, you've met your first drop bear.

faq.a: Nope. It's a joke Australians tell visitors and there's no animal that drops out of trees onto people. The closest real thing was the marsupial lion, Thylacoleo carnifex, and it died out tens of thousands of years ago.

faq.q: What is the drop bear's scientific name?
faq.a: The joke name is Thylarctos plummetus, from the Australian Museum's spoof entry. It roughly means "pouched bear that plummets". It's not a real species (sorry).

faq.q: Do koalas ever drop on people?
faq.a: Not on purpose. Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves and stay away from people. They'll scratch and bite if you grab one, and now and then one falls or climbs down a tree by a path, but they don't hunt anything.
In the joke, in gum trees along bush tracks anywhere in Australia, and especially around places tourists go. Some people say they're worst in Queensland and New South Wales.

faq.q: Is the drop bear like the jackalope?
faq.a: Yes, same idea. Both are tall tales for outsiders, kept going by locals with straight faces and a lot of souvenirs. The [jackalope](/creatures/jackalope/) is the American version and the [hoop snake](/creatures/hoop-snake/) is another classic.
